newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-EX-CHAMPIONS SEARCH FOR FORM AT BRITISH OPEN.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-EX-CHAMPIONS SEARCH FOR FORM AT BRITISH OPEN.

text.p: TROON, Scotland, July 17 - Two former British Open champions would regard it as something of an achievement if they survived the halfway cut in this year's tournament which starts on Thursday.
Ill-health and poor form have dogged both three-time winner Severiano Ballesteros and Ian Baker-Finch who took the title in 1991.

Baker-Finch's game has deteriorated so much that he has not even played in a tournament since the British Open 12 months ago and Ballesteros, while playing regularly on the European Tour, has missed the halfway cut in 10 out of the 12 tournaments he has played this year.

It has been a tragic comedown for the charismatic Spaniard who for several periods in the late 1980s was the world number one and as well as his three British Opens had also won the U.S. Masters twice.

But then his game began to fall away as increasing back trouble caused him to make alterations to his swing. He was continually searching for that elusive 'something' to put back the magical touch into his game.
He even took a five-month sabbatical from the game at the end of the 1995 season to see if that would make an improvement. It made little difference.
But the 40-year-old Spaniard refuses to give in and two months ago he was insisting he could still qualify for a playing place on Europe's Ryder Cup team, of which he is captain.

His determination to rediscover his form is clear for anyone to see. After missing the cut at last week's world invitational at Loch Lomond, Ballesteros spent several hours being coached on the driving range.
The 36-year-old Baker-Finch's fall has been even more dramatic and on Wednesday he admitted he had spent a sleepless night agonising over whether to pull out of the Open.
His slump in form caused him to quit America where he had been playing on the U.S. Tour and move back to his native Australia where now he plays only social golf.

The source of his trouble has also been a back injury and he has to take anti-inflammatory pills before playing. He admits he is not 100 percent fit but his family and friends persuaded him to play on Thursday although he is clearly nervous at the prospect.
"When you're feeling 100 percent and you've been playing well and you've been playing tournament golf, it's still a bloody hard game," he said.
Both players have the sympathy of all their fellow professionals. Many have paid tribute to them this week for their courage in refusing to give up.
Fellow Australian Greg Norman said of Baker-Finch: "Everybody who plays the game of golf hates to see a player of that calibre as low as he is.

"I feel I know a little bit about him, every player knows a lot about him because we've all been through a slump. When you've hit the bottom it just depends how much fortitude you've got to come back out of that.

"He's got to climb that mountain all over again. But he's still got the skills, he's got the memory of winning at Royal Birkdale. He's still got the memory of winning all the other golf tournaments he has, and he's got the support of every player out here."

The world number three added: "It's the same with Seve. We hate to see it, we really do, because they are both great for the game of golf. We would love to see the 126th British Open have them play to the level that they've played in the past.

"That would be wonderful, because both these guys, the British Open made both of them and it would be wonderful to see the British Open turn it all around for them. And the only way it can do it is if they play."
